title: What makes Mysore rasam powder different
excerpt: Karnataka rasam leans on pepper, not chilli. Here is why that one choice changes the whole bowl.
html:
Rasam — saaru in Karnataka — is meant to be light and drinkable, not a heavy gravy. The difference comes down to one decision: pepper leads, chilli supports.

Pepper first

A Mysore-style blend is built around black pepper and cumin, with just enough Byadagi chilli for colour. Byadagi is deep red but mild, so you get the look of heat without the burn.

Why fillers ruin it

Many commercial powders bulk out the blend with roasted lentils. That thickens the rasam and mutes the aroma. A true rasam powder is only spices.

Getting it right at home

Boil tamarind water with tomato, stir in a spoon of powder near the end, and finish with a ghee tempering. Adding the powder too early cooks off the aroma you paid for.

seo.title: Mysore Rasam Powder: why pepper matters more than chilli
seo.description: Karnataka rasam is pepper-forward, not chilli-heavy. What goes into an authentic Mysore rasam powder, why fillers ruin it, and how to use it.

title: How to store spice powders so they stay fragrant
excerpt: Freshly ground masala loses aroma faster than you think. Six habits that keep it alive for months.
html:
Preservative-free masala has a shorter, honest shelf life. Aroma is the first thing to go, and it goes quietly.

Airtight, always

Move the powder into a glass or steel jar the day it arrives. Every time a pouch is opened and resealed, some aroma leaves with the air.

Do not refrigerate

The fridge feels sensible and is not. Condensation forms each time the jar comes out, and moisture clumps the powder and dulls the oils.

Keep it away from the stove

A shelf right above the hob is the worst place in the kitchen: heat and steam both age the blend.

If the aroma fades

Dry roast a spoonful for a few seconds before use. It will not be new again, but it wakes up considerably.

seo.description: How to store ground masala and chutney powder so it stays fragrant: airtight jars, no refrigeration, away from heat and steam.

title: Byadagi vs Guntur: choosing your chilli
excerpt: One brings colour, the other brings heat. Most Karnataka blends use both, in a particular ratio.
html:
Ask why one sambar is glowing red and another is merely brown, and the answer is usually the chilli.

Byadagi: colour without burn

Grown in northern Karnataka, Byadagi is wrinkled, deep red and remarkably mild. It is used for colour, and it is why a Karnataka sambar looks richer than its heat suggests.

Guntur: the heat

Guntur, from Andhra Pradesh, is the opposite — sharp, direct heat and far less colour.

The ratio

Most household blends sit somewhere near three parts Byadagi to one part Guntur. Shift it toward Guntur and you get a hotter, duller-looking blend; shift it the other way and it looks striking but tastes flat.

seo.title: Byadagi vs Guntur chillies: colour, heat and the right ratio
seo.description: Byadagi gives Karnataka masalas their deep red colour; Guntur brings the heat. How the two differ and what ratio traditional blends use.
